title: X Tells Delhi High Court an Impostor Sent Fake Takedown Notices Targeting IFF and SFLC
excerpt: X said the notices seeking removal of the Internet Freedom Foundation and SFLC.in accounts were not sent by the Delhi Police, that it had not acted on them, and that it has complained to the police about the impersonation.
body:
• X told the Delhi High Court on November 6 that takedown notices against the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and SFLC.in were sent by an impostor impersonating the Delhi Police, not by the police themselves.
  • X said it had not acted on the notices, had carried out an internal investigation, and had filed a complaint with the Delhi Police the previous night.
  • The second notice covered 40 URLs, including 37 posts and the entire X accounts of IFF, SFLC.in and GeoBlockedIndia, alleging defamation of the RSS under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
  • Justice Amit Mahajan recorded X's statement and disposed of both organisations' petitions, with liberty to approach the court again if X acts on the notices.

The takedown notices that threatened the X accounts of two of India's best-known digital-rights groups were fake. X told the Delhi High Court on Friday, November 6, that the notices, submitted in the name of a senior Delhi Police officer, were sent by an impostor, according to MediaNama's account of the hearing and Bar and Bench.

"It turns out this was somebody playing an impostor, somebody impersonating Delhi Police who has sent this. We are not actioning this request because it's an illegal request. It's not from Delhi Police. We filed a complaint last night with Delhi Police."

— Counsel for X, Delhi High Court

What the notices demanded

X had forwarded the reports to the affected users on November 3, saying in the interest of transparency that it had received requests from the Delhi Police about their accounts. The reports named Hargobinder Singh Dhaliwal, Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), as the sender. The second report listed 40 URLs: 37 individual posts and the entire accounts of the Internet Freedom Foundation, SFLC.in and GeoBlockedIndia, and it also sought removal of posts by 16 other users who had commented on the controversy, Bar and Bench reported.

The stated ground was defamation of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which covers criminal defamation. IFF's own account of the episode, published by the Internet Freedom Foundation, says the first report was submitted through X's public online reporting form on October 31 and the second on November 2, and that the second invoked a rule requiring platforms to act on lawful notices within three hours.

Why the groups went to court

Senior Advocate Akhil Sibal, appearing for both organisations, told the court they had doubted the notices from the start and had written to the authorities seeking confirmation, MediaNama reported. SFLC.in's email to the address given in the notices bounced back as undeliverable, and neither the Delhi Police nor X gave a confirmation before the petitions were filed. Sibal argued that criminal defamation is a non-cognisable offence, which raised the question of how police could issue such a notice at all, and the petitions contended that seeking removal of entire accounts was disproportionate and violated freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).

An advocate for the Delhi Police attended the hearing but made no submissions, MediaNama reported.

What the court decided, and what remains open

After X clarified that the notices were fake, Sibal submitted that X's statement could be recorded and the petitions disposed of. Justice Amit Mahajan recorded the statement and closed both petitions, giving the organisations liberty to approach the court afresh if X takes any action against their accounts or posts, IFF said.

The immediate threat to the three accounts is therefore lifted, and X says it is not likely to act on the reports. What is not settled is who submitted them. Someone was able to file two reports with a major platform in the name of a serving Special Commissioner of Police, using an address in the police's name, and place three organisations and 16 other users under a three-hour removal threat, IFF noted. That impersonation is now the subject of X's complaint to the Delhi Police, which had made no public statement about the reports before the hearing.
nri_angle: The case shows how easily an official-looking takedown demand can threaten lawful speech online — a verification problem for platforms, newsrooms and diaspora-run digital-rights groups alike.
author: Diaspora Desk
